chapter_theme: Akananuru 301-320 (from the Nithilakkovai) alternate paalai poems of the man gone for wealth and the road he takes (bandits, carrion crows, a dove that will not leave a ruined hall) with kurinji and neythal poems in which the friend refuses or redirects the secret meetings and presses for marriage, two marutham poems on the courtesan quarrel, and two mullai poems of the rains and the return; wandering performers and the fame of Paari, Pulli, Vaanavan and the Pandya Vazhuthi supply the similes.

301.reading: Answering the friend who says she has borne her absent lover's memory fairly well, the heroine says each returning evening is as desolate as an old town's commons on the day after a troupe of wandering performers, who spend their wages without saving and roam with drums, pipes and flower garlands from town to town, has danced there and moved on; so how could the love he gave be forgotten just because he stays away long?
301.nuance: Twenty lines celebrate the performers' rootless, music-filled life only so that their absence can be felt: the joy is drawn at length to measure the emptiness it leaves. The troupe always leaves, as evening always comes back, so the desolation is a daily one. The word மறுவினம் (line 26) is obscure to me; I read it as the evening that comes round again.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine endures her lover's absence; the performers' road is a wasteland road

comparisons.tenor: the heroine wilting in longing, like a crop in a field struck by drought
the open mouth of the performers' grass-roofed cart
the long and short pipes joined with the drum
the beat they set, like frogs croaking on the water when the rain clouds thunder

comparisons.vehicle: புன்றலை மன்றங் காணின் வழிநாள் அழுங்கன் மூதூர்க்கு இன்னா தாகும் அதுவே
comparisons.tenor: the evening that returns each day

302.reading: With the hero listening outside, the friend tells the heroine that bathing in the falls with the lord of the hills where plantain leaves stroke a sleeping elephant's back, picking blue lilies in the pool and playing in the fragrant vengai grove all seem to have become hard, for though the millet their brothers sowed has ripened enough to draw the parrots, their unkind mother shows no sign of sending them out to guard it and keeps looking at the girl's swelling breasts and thick hair.
302.nuance: The millet and the girl ripen together, and both end the field-guarding that made the day meetings possible: the mother's watching eyes mean confinement at home. Spoken for the hero to overhear, the friend's complaint tells him that only marriage is left. The plantain leaf stroking the sleeping elephant (lines 1 to 3) may suggest the tenderness of the hills' lord, but the leaf moves with the wind and does no act, so I leave it as scene.

colophon.thurai: பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field guarded from parrots and the hill falls

comparisons.tenor: the tall millet with heavy ears, handsome as sugarcane

303.reading: The heroine scolds her foolish heart: their love, hidden from all like a ghoul's dream, was exposed by gossip loud as the cascade on Porayan's Kolli hill, and the man left; yet the heart believed he would come back as surely as the sparrows of Paari's Parambu fly off at dawn for red paddy and return together at dusk; let it be rid of that doubt, for she has resolved to follow his road across the wasteland, as fish leave a draining pool.
303.nuance: The Paari simile is turned against the heart that made it: sparrows return every evening, he has not. The last image reverses the direction of the poem: not he comes back to her, but she leaves, as fish leave water that is running out, the town that gossip has drained. The resolve is spoken to her own heart and may not be meant to be carried out.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேட்கை மீதூர்ந்த தலைமகள் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a heroine left behind, resolving to cross the wasteland after him

comparisons.tenor: their hidden love, unseen by others

comparisons.vehicle: கொல்லி யுச்சித் தாஅய்த் ததைந்துசெல் அருவியின் அலர்எழ
comparisons.tenor: the gossip that rose about them
the elephants Paari gives, huge as hills
his expected return
the cicadas shrilling on dead trees
her going after him

occasion.words: வேட்கை மீதூர்ந்த தலைமகள் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

304.reading: In the war camp, as the first rains fall at dawn and the land takes on the season's beauty, the doe with her fawn resting with the stag in the kurunthu shade, peacocks dancing and kaayaa flowers strewn among red velvet mites like coral set among sapphires, the hero tells his heart that his dark wife, not knowing his own pain, must be saying that a man who lingers abroad on the king's work has no righteousness and no grace, and sulking at him.
304.nuance: He hears himself judged in her words (lines 18 and 19: அறவர் அல்லர் நம் அருளாதோர்) and does not argue; his only defence, that she cannot know his pain, is also a confession that the season's beauty is hurting him too.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season and the scrub flowers of the forest

comparisons.tenor: the hailstones
the red earth, as if wrought
the clear pooled water
blue kaayaa flowers among red mites on the sand

iraicchi.act: the doe with her fawn rests beside the stag in the shade when the rains come
iraicchi.sense: even the deer are together at the season of return, which is exactly what makes his staying away graceless in her eyes

305.reading: The heroine tells her friend that on these cold midnights of north wind and drizzle, when the night will not pass, even lovers locked in an embrace that seems to drink each other and enter each other's bodies feel lonely; so how is she to live, now that the graceless man is going away for wealth, when the pained cry of a lone anril on the palmyra stirs her smouldering heart and the herdsmen's sweet flute blows it into flame?
305.nuance: An argument from the stronger case: if the embraced suffer such nights, the one left alone cannot bear them. The flute-players are நினையா மாக்கள், people who do not think: the music is innocent and only her heart turns it into a bellows. The lone anril, a bird famed for never leaving its mate, may carry more than its cry, but it acts here only as a sound, so I leave it as scene.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is leaving for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' desire, as if drinking each other
the embrace, as if entering the body
the flute fanning her smouldering longing

306.reading: Turning the reveller away from the door, the friend mocks his fine reputation: a woman with a moon-bright forehead has just scolded him, looked at him with reddened, tearful eyes, torn off his cool garland in a quarrel and walked away through their own street.
306.nuance: The rival performs in public the oodal that the wife is refused, and does it in front of the wife's house; the friend needs no other reason to shut the door. The well-fed heron asleep under stroking mango shoots and the tortoise basking on the cane (lines 2 to 7) may hint at the pampered hero, but only one correspondence maps clearly, so I keep them as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: a quarrel over another woman, in the watered fields

comparisons.tenor: the other woman's bright forehead

307.reading: The friend asks the man set on his work whether he can leave without thinking how the girl here will suffer, her forehead pale, her shoulders thin, her tears falling like rain on flowers, when the mountain road he means to take runs past a ruined hall overgrown with bushes where, on the black pillar the god has abandoned, a dove still calls with its mate, unable to leave because they have lived there together so long.
307.nuance: The dove clings to a home that even its god has deserted; the man is about to desert a living one. The road's other creatures, the must-maddened tusker that killed a tiger and the bears digging out termites, make it frightening; the dove makes it a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend tries to stop a departure for work

comparisons.tenor: her tearful eyes

iraicchi.act: the dove stays with its mate on the pillar of a ruined hall and will not leave it, because of their long life there together
iraicchi.sense: a bird will not desert an old shared home even when its god has gone, so a man should not leave the woman he has lived with

308.reading: The friend asks the lord of the rain-washed hills, where a tusker still carries the long wound of its fight with a tiger and white clouds wrap the mountain like smoke from a potter's kiln, why he comes at night: let him come by day, chase parrots from the millet with them on the high platform of their spear-bearing father, sleep pillowed on her hair dressed with lilies from the rock pools, and at dusk slip past the guards like a raiding tusker back to his village of kurinji shrubs.
308.nuance: The opening wounded tusker shows the night road's danger without saying so. The day offer is not simple: the field is guarded, the father carries an 'unfailing spear', and the hero must leave like a crop-raiding elephant, so the day meeting carries its own risk. The colophon names only the request to come by day.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet platform and the parrots of the hill field

comparisons.tenor: white clouds wrapping the mountain
the hero slipping away from the guarded field

309.reading: The heroine asks her friend, who has grown sad at seeing her change, why they should not set out, as wandering performers set out for the Chera Vaanavan's feet without counting the forest long, through a land where Mazhavar raiders drive off milch cattle and feast on a cow killed at the god's neem tree, to the country beyond the hills where he went, where a night-raiding elephant takes fright at dawn.
309.nuance: She borrows the performers' courage: the gift-seekers cross the raiders' forest for a patron, so she can cross it for her man. The closing lines (the cracking bamboo, the sling and the elephant afraid of the thicket) are obscure to me and the reading of them is a guess.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு வேறுபட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine proposes to follow the man across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the white seeds of the silk-cotton scattering

comparisons.vehicle: கோடியர் பெரும்படைக் குதிரை நற்போர் வானவன் திருந்துகழற் சேவடி நசைஇப் படர்ந்தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the heroine's going after her man

310.reading: Having agreed to help the man who has sent his chariot and men away and come humbly pleading for many days, the friend tells him that the girl too is deeply moved, but as a daughter raised in love in her mother's house she is still shy and innocent, so he must not press here today; let him go to the calling-place under the palmyra above the flowering punnai, near their small village fenced by the roaring sea.
310.nuance: The friend grants his suit by naming a place, not by bringing the girl: the meeting is set within call of the village, where the girl's innocence and the friend's control are both kept. Where exactly she sends him (கூஉம்கண், the bird of line 15) is not clear to me.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore, its trees and salt traders

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes
the heaped dunes, looking like hills

311.reading: The friend reminds the heroine how he once waited at the painted, guarded door like gift-seekers waiting for an elephant, came in at midnight when the guards slept, swore that no one in this world surpassed her and stroked her hair for days; so though he has crossed the scorched wasteland beyond Pulli's good land, where herdsmen share sweet tamarind food with travellers on teak leaves, the man who left her with gracious assurances will not stay long.
311.nuance: The friend's proof is the past: a man who waited at the door like a suppliant for a gift will not linger away from the gift itself. The herdsmen's hospitality softens the road she fears.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: his waiting at the door of her house
the strong door, as if painted

312.reading: The friend, letting the hero overhear, says that if he means to marry and end the hardship of night visits they will rejoice, and tomorrow, careless of the village's gossip, bathe in the flood coming down the hill with his chest for their float, for the rain has come down over the bamboo slopes, roaring like a drum and flashing lightning like the spear the victorious Pandya Vazhuthi raises in battle.
312.nuance: The public bath with the lover is promised on a condition (வரையக் கருதும் ஆயின்): only marriage makes the gossip harmless. The storm borrows a king's victory to make the coming flood, and the union it stands for, triumphal.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது. தலைமகள் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill village and its slopes

comparisons.tenor: the hero's chest as their float
the thundering rain

comparisons.vehicle: வெல்போர் வழுதி செல்சமத் துயர்த்த அடுபுகழ் எஃகம் போல
comparisons.tenor: the lightning

313.reading: The friend tells the heroine, who weeps night and day, sighs hot breaths and has lost her forehead's glow like a moon swallowed by the snake, that the man who held her close saying 'what else is there now? do not fear', though he left for wealth across rock-piled hills where starving snakes shrink like emptied purses and crows drink the blood of travellers shot down by bandits, will come back out of grace.
313.nuance: The friend's comfort rests on his own quoted words (line 1); the road she describes in full is the danger she argues past. The crows that drink quietly, like spies in a deserted place, are the poem's chilling detail.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: her tear-filled eyes
her dimmed forehead
the starving snake, shrunk
the crows' hushed calls

314.reading: The friend welcomes the hero home from finished work: in the rains, as the stag frisked in the green crops with his doe and fawn and the lute played its evening melody of grief, his wife of godlike chastity had asked the bard what would become of her if he did not come now, and he arrived in time to end her grief; so may his garland flourish and his chest, held by the young woman whose hair smells of the white mullai on the fence, last for ever.
314.nuance: The mullai on the fence comes back in her hair at the end: the flower of the land of waiting becomes the scent of the embrace. Her question is reported in her own words, so the friend's praise is also a record of how near the despair was.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season in the scrub forest

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds

iraicchi.act: the stag holds close his doe with her fawn and frisks with them in the green crops when the rains come
iraicchi.sense: the season that keeps the deer family together is the season the husband was bound to come home to his wife

315.reading: The mother whose daughter has gone off with her lover blames herself: she saw the girl's hair curl and breasts swell and even yesterday suspected, yet did not shut her in; and now the girl, who had not yet stepped out of a house guarded like Vazhuthi's city of Koodal, follows the lying spearman over a summer path strewn with green gooseberries like crystal beads from a broken string, and will sleep, perhaps, in a forest hamlet where meat is cooked before huts like heaped teak leaves.
315.nuance: I read சிலம்புங் கழியாள் (line 8) as 'she whose anklets were not yet removed': the girl has gone before the anklet ceremony that comes before a wedding, so the mother counts the rite the elopement skipped. She calls the young man a deceiver (பொய்ப்ப), which is her view, not the poem's verdict.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's going away with her lover across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: her rising breasts, rivalling caskets
her well-guarded home
green gooseberries dropping on bare ground
the forest-dwellers' huts

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: the mother speaks her grief aloud

316.reading: The friend, having agreed to let in the hero, whose chariot keeps bringing courtesans, asks the wife whether she can afford to sulk in vain because he cannot give them up, since women who were able to keep up their sulking ended alone when fortune left them, sifting and cooking a little food for themselves while their sweet-voiced sons sucked shrunken breasts, and others still do not learn from it.
316.nuance: Unusually blunt: the friend argues from the household's livelihood, not from love. The opening buffalo, which grazes the lilies, sleeps in the mud and comes home at dusk crowned with pakanrai, carries the hero's conduct without naming it.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்கு வாயில் நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளை நெருங்கிச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan quarrel of the watered country

comparisons.tenor: the buffalo striding into the old town

ullurai.tenor: the husband who spends his days with courtesans and comes home at evening

pairs.situation: he has taken his pleasure among the courtesans
he lies at ease in their quarter all day
he comes home at dusk wearing their garlands

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a marutham buffalo of the hero's own town in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

317.reading: The friend tells the heroine that while they sat looking out and wondering whether the season he had named had failed to come where he was, the season he promised when he said he would come back to hear the koel in the mango with her, in lovely spring when the palasa buds redden like dyed nails and bees and humming insects shake down the kuravam and kongu blossoms, her lover has come and stands here, as swiftly as the heart goes to what it longs for; so where now is the pallor that spread on her forehead for so many days, until even her mother noticed?
317.nuance: The long spring catalogue (lines 1 to 17) is the hero's own promise, quoted, so the description of the season is also the evidence that his word was kept. The final question treats the pallor as already gone.

thinai_evidence.note: the spring term set for the return from a parting

comparisons.tenor: the daytime gloom of the cold season
the sharp red palasa buds
blossoms falling as the bees work them
the humming of the thumbi
the mango thick with blossom
the lover's sudden arrival

318.reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich hills, who comes alone at night by a narrow path where elephants walk, thunder roars and snakes and tigers make it fearful, that marriage he can have if he wants it, but from today he must not come; and if he does come, then when he has left her and reached his own rocky village, he must blow the horn that calls together his hunting dogs, so that they, left here in anxiety, know he is safe.
318.nuance: The ban and the care sit in one breath: the friend who forbids the visits still needs to hear the horn. மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை makes marriage sound easily granted, which takes away his reason for the night road.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை வரவு விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill path, its beasts and falls

comparisons.tenor: the bees humming to the song of the falls

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை வரவு விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது

319.reading: The friend tells the man who has announced his journey that if he means to leave her, the girl whose look strikes like a goddess, slim-waisted, her breasts freckled like new vengai blossom, for a wasteland where flocks of crows on the banyan call over the hunters' forts and carry off the corpses of travellers shot by raiders, then may he get his rare wealth: she, tender as a fresh shoot, young and full of love, has not even the boldness to answer his 'we will go' with 'then we will stay behind'.
319.nuance: The blessing (எய்துக மாதோ நுமக்கே) is a curse in form. The two descriptions weigh against each other: the carrion road and her beauty. The last line may also be read as 'she cannot say she will die', since ஒழிவேம் can mean both; either way it is her silence that the friend speaks for.

thinai_evidence.note: a departure for wealth that the friend tries to prevent

comparisons.tenor: her glance
the freckles on her breasts
the girl herself

320.reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore, where the fishermen's catch is cried for sale by their well-dressed sisters in the festive streets, why he shows no grace to free her friend's grief from gossiping mouths: even if he lies now, was the oath also false that he swore on the day he first came in his tall chariot, its wheels crushing the girls' sand dolls, to the ford dusted with punnai pollen where the swan preens on the dunes, and first held her? The sea knows; it was the witness.
320.nuance: The chariot that ruins the girls' sand dolls (line 12) on the day of the first meeting reads to me as the end of her girlhood, though nothing in the poem says so. Calling the sea as witness makes the shore itself the court where his oath stands.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishing hamlet and the shore grove

comparisons.tenor: her friend's kohl-lined eyes

links.note: Both use the wandering kodiyar troupe: in 301 their leaving empties a town's commons, and that emptiness is the heroine's evening; in 309 their going to Vaanavan is the model for the heroine's own journey after her man.
links.teaches: The same performers figure both sides of parting, the place left desolate and the traveller who will not count the forest long, so akam poets used the bards' life as a ready picture of both staying and going.

links.note: Akananuru 303 calls Paari the giver of hill-like elephants to any suppliant and makes his Parambu the place sparrows always return to at evening; Purananuru 108 says Paari never answers a suppliant with 'I will not come'.
links.teaches: The akam poet borrows the certainty of Paari's giving, famous from the puram poems, to make the sparrows' return seem certain, so that the heroine's disappointment is measured against a patron who never failed anyone.

links.note: Both open in the first rains with a stag, a doe and her fawn together; in 304 the hero sees them from the war camp and imagines his wife's reproach, in 314 the friend sees them as the hero comes home in time.
links.teaches: One scene of the deer family carries reproach while he is away and fulfilment when he returns, which shows that what a karu thing implies is fixed by the uri of the poem, not by the thing itself.

links.note: Both picture a public hall (பொதியில்) fallen to ruin, its pillar abandoned by its god; in Purananuru 52 it is the fate of lands the Pandya conquers, in Akananuru 307 a dove clings to it with its mate.
links.teaches: A ruined hall abandoned by its god was a stock picture of a conquered land, and the akam poet turns it round: even in that ruin a pair of birds keeps faith, which makes the hero's leaving harsher.

links.note: The same poet, Maruthan Ilanagan, praises Vazhuthi's war in Purananuru 52 and in Akananuru 312 likens lightning to the spear Vazhuthi raises against fleeing enemies.
links.teaches: One poet's war praise for a Pandya becomes, in his love poem, the measure of a storm's power, showing puram fame travelling into akam as a simile that its first hearers would recognise.

links.note: Both describe the waterless road where bowmen shoot travellers and birds feed on the dead; in Purananuru 3 suppliants brave it for the Pandya's gifts, in Akananuru 313 the husband crosses it for wealth.
links.teaches: The same death road is crossed for the same motive, gain, by the suppliant and by the husband; puram counts the crossing as praise of the patron, akam as the measure of what the wife fears.

links.note: Both are the friend telling the wife not to prolong her sulking: Kural 1302 says sulking is salt and too much spoils it; Akananuru 316 shows women who sulked too long left alone, poor and nursing hungry sons.
links.teaches: What the Kural calls spoiling by too much salt the Sangam friend spells out as the loss of fortune and household, so the couplet's measured image stands for a social and economic ruin, not only a lost pleasure.

links.note: Both are the friend turning back a man who comes at night by a beast-haunted hill path: in 308 she offers day meetings instead, in 318 she bans his visits and offers marriage.
links.teaches: Read in order, the two refusals show the stages of the friend's pressure: first moving the meeting to day, still within secret love, then closing the meetings so that marriage is the only road left.

links.note: Both are spoken to a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell me if you are not going, and keep your promise of a quick return for those who will still be alive; Akananuru 319's friend says go and get your wealth, since the girl cannot even say she will stay behind.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem shows why the friend speaks in this situation at all: the girl is too young and loving to answer him herself, which supports reading the couplet's 'tell me' as the friend speaking for her.

source_issues: 304: the colophon thurai begins with a stray numeral (1பாசறைக்கண்), a footnote marker left in the text.
304: line 12 spells peacock மஞ்ஜை with the grantha ஜ; the usual form is மஞ்ஞை, probably a digitisation error.
305: line 5 is missing from the base text and was supplied from the commentary edition (flag); marked as supplied.
319: the base text prints the poem number as 318 (flag); read as 319.
301: line 26 மறுவினம் is obscure; the comparison of the evening to the emptied commons turns on it.
311: line 11 தீரத reads oddly before தேக்கிலை (one would expect தீரத்); possibly a misprint, marked as it stands.
